title: Violets by the fence
translation: The flower of someone's heart can fade before the wind even touches it. You think of the years you spent close. Every word that moved you is still with you. And yet they drift out of your life. That's sadder than losing someone to death.
That's why, in the old Chinese stories, one man wept over white thread because it could be dyed any colour, and another wept at a crossroads because the paths split there.
Among the hundred poems written for Emperor Horikawa, there's this one:

The fence of the girl I used to see
has gone to ruin.
Only violets now,
in among the wild grass.
So lonely. The poet must have lived through something like that.
original: {風|かぜ}も{吹|ふ}きあへず{移|うつ}ろふ{人|ひと}の{心|こころ}の{花|はな}に、{馴|な}れにし{年月|としつき}をおもへば、あはれと{聞|き}きし{言|こと}の{葉|は}ごとに{忘|わす}れぬものから、{我|わ}が{世|よ}の{外|ほか}になり{行|ゆ}くならひこそ、{亡|な}き{人|ひと}の{別|わか}れよりも{勝|まさ}りて{悲|かな}しきものなれ。
されば{白|しろ}き{糸|いと}の{染|そ}まむ{事|こと}を{悲|かな}しび、{道|みち}の{衢|ちまた}のわかれむ{事|こと}を{歎|なげ}く{人|ひと}もありけむかし。
{堀河院|ほりかはのゐん}の{百首|ひやくしゆ}の{歌|うた}の{中|うち}に、
むかし{見|み}し{妹|いも}が{垣根|かきね}は{荒|あ}れにけり{茅花|つばな}まじりの{菫|すみれ}のみして
さびしきけしき、さること{侍|はべ}りけむ。
literal: Thinking of the years one was close, with the flower of a person's heart that fades even before the wind has blown, though one does not forget each word one heard as moving, the way they become outside one's own world is sadder even than parting from the dead.
So there must have been people who grieved that white thread would be dyed, and lamented that the paths at a crossroads would part.
Among the hundred poems of (the reign of) Emperor Horikawa,
'The fence of the girl I once saw has gone to ruin; with only violets mixed among the cogon grass'
the lonely scene: something like that must have happened.

notes.text: 'The flower of a person's heart', from a famous Kokinshū poem by Ono no Komachi: what fades without any visible colour is the flower of the human heart. The heart changes faster than any blossom.

notes.quote: 我が世の外になり行く
notes.text: 'Becoming outside my world': not death, but the slow drift of someone who is still alive. Kenkō says this is worse than death.

notes.quote: 白き糸の染まむ事を悲しび
notes.text: Two Chinese stories. Mozi wept at white silk thread, because it would take whatever colour it was dyed. Yang Zhu wept at a crossroads, because one step could lead to completely different places. Both are about people changing, and about partings.
A collection of a hundred poems each by a group of poets, presented to Emperor Horikawa around 1105. This poem is usually attributed to Fujiwara no Kinzane.
{茅花|つばな}: the flowering cogon grass, a weed. {妹|いも}: a man's word for the woman he loves. The fence of her house is overgrown, so she no longer lives there.
